analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to regulate cigarettes: mandatory ingredient disclosure, tougher warnings, a candy-flavor ban, and limits on youth advertising.
analysis.headline: Fifty-nine senators, including 13 Republicans, cosponsored the bill and the Senate health committee approved it in August 2007, but it never came to a floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have handed the Food and Drug Administration authority over tobacco products for the first time [S2]. Cigarette makers would have to register, disclose ingredients and harmful constituents, open plants to inspection, and submit new products for approval before sale [S2]. It would ban candy, fruit, and spice flavorings designed to appeal to young smokers, allow stronger warning labels, restrict advertising aimed at youth, and let the FDA recall unreasonably harmful products, funded by fees on manufacturers [S2]. It explicitly leaves tobacco legal: FDA could not ban products or cut nicotine to zero — only Congress could — could not require a prescription, could not bar retail outlets from selling, and could not set the purchase age above 18 [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Children, who would face fewer candy-flavored cigarettes and fewer ads aimed at them [S3]; smokers, who would get full ingredient and constituent disclosure, revised warning labels, and honest rules for "reduced risk" claims [S2]; and the public, which the bill's own findings say would save roughly $75 billion in health costs from halving youth smoking [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Kids, smokers, and the public's health

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA authority over tobacco products, with registration, inspection, recordkeeping, disclosure, and user fee requirements for manufacturers [S2].
Requires companies to report all ingredients, nicotine delivery, and harmful constituents, and to hand over internal research on health effects of their products [S3].
Bans characterizing flavors other than tobacco and menthol — including strawberry, grape, clove, cinnamon, cocoa, and coffee — that make cigarettes more appealing to new, young users [S3].

Requires premarket approval of new tobacco products, allows the Secretary to restrict advertising and promotion to protect public health, and gives the FDA power to publicly notify consumers and order recalls of unreasonably harmful products [S2].
Revises and strengthens the warning labels on cigarettes and smokeless tobacco, with authority for the Secretary to update them over time [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would pay user fees, disclose previously secret product data, absorb compliance and premarket-approval costs, and lose the flavored-cigarette market [S2][S3]; much of that would likely reach adult smokers as higher prices, since fees and compliance costs get built into what the consumer pays [S2].

drawbacks.text: The flavor ban explicitly exempts menthol [S3] — the one flavor most used by Black American smokers — so the largest menthol brands stay fully on the market untouched, a carve-out widely attributed to industry influence.

Existing products are effectively grandfathered: premarket approval applies to products not marketed as of June 1, 2003 [S3], which raises barriers for new entrants and new reduced-risk products while incumbents' brands continue without review — the likely reason the largest cigarette maker supported the bill.

The bill preserves tobacco's legality by design: FDA cannot ban any product or reduce nicotine to zero (that power is reserved to Congress), cannot require prescriptions, cannot bar a category of retail outlet from selling, and cannot set a purchase age above 18 [S2].
New user fees on manufacturers [S2] would likely be passed through to consumers as higher cigarette prices, falling on the adult smokers the bill keeps fully legal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain was explicit legality, the menthol carve-out, and a grandfather clause for existing brands — in exchange for the first real federal oversight of the deadliest consumer product. For most public-health advocates the trade was clearly worth taking, and 59 senators signed on. But the carve-outs show concentrated interests shaping the fine print: the flavor most used by Black smokers was spared, and the rules were written so that today's dominant brands face no premarket review while newcomers do.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved it in August 2007, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a floor vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced S. 625 on February 15, 2007, with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including Republicans John McCain, John Cornyn, Richard Lugar, Olympia Snowe, Susan Collins, and Lisa Murkowski [S3].
It drew 59 cosponsors in all: 44 Democrats, 13 Republicans, and 2 independents [S4].
The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee held hearings on the bill on February 27, 2007 [S5].
On August 1, 2007, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute — a step short of passage [S5].
The Senate never voted on the bill; its last recorded action was the favorable committee report, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, cigarette companies that opposed regulation were spared FDA oversight, ingredient disclosure, advertising limits, and user fees for the rest of the Congress, and the public got none of the projected reductions in youth smoking or tobacco-related disease.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines — 59 cosponsors including 13 Republicans and 2 independents — while the blocking came mostly from tobacco-state members, so the fight did not split cleanly by party.

industries.note: The bill imposes registration, biennial inspections, ingredient and constituent disclosure, records demands, premarket approval for new products, stricter warnings, advertising restrictions, and user fees [S2][S3]. The industry's loss is exactly the public health gain the bill sought — which is why its foes fought it.

The bill grandfathered products already on the market as of June 1, 2003 — premarket review applies only to new items [S3] — and a giant incumbent can absorb compliance costs that smaller rivals cannot. Publicly backing regulation would lock in its dominance even as it accepted oversight, which is why the market leader supported the bill while smaller competitors opposed it.

The flavor ban lists banned characterizing flavors but explicitly exempts menthol [S3], sparing the flavor most used by Black American smokers. The carve-out protects the biggest menthol brands while candy and clove flavored products are banned outright.

The bill guarantees that regulators cannot prohibit face-to-face sales by any category of retail outlet and cannot set the purchase age above 18 [S2], preserving retailers' legal sales channel — the same access that sustains youth uptake.
